scope.end: 31b: R. Shmuel bar R. Yitzchak asks whence we know that God conceded to Elijah — the answer appears on 32a

sections.title: Rav Hamnuna: Halakhot Drawn from Hannah's Verses
sections.gist: From a few verses of Hannah's prayer the Gemara extracts a chain of laws — three rules of prayer, the ban on praying drunk, and a series of obligations between people.

bullets.text: Rav Hamnuna: *kamah hilkheta gavraveta ika lemishma mehanei kerai deChanah* — how many significant *halakhot* can be derived from these verses of Hannah (I Samuel 1:13–17).

Strikingly, only the first few derivations concern prayer itself; the majority are interpersonal — to rebuke, to judge favorably, to clear a false suspicion, to appease and to bless. Ethics between people is drawn out of a narrative about standing before God.

The passage follows directly on the description of R. Akiva's prayer: communal prayer is clipped and restrained, private prayer is the arena of *kavanah* — and Hannah is the model for the private mode.

chart.caption: Each phrase of the Hannah narrative and the law derived from it
rows: One who prays must focus his heart
One must enunciate the words with the lips
One may not raise his voice in the *Amidah*
A drunk person may not pray
One who sees unseemly behavior must reprimand
One wrongly suspected must clear himself
*Al titen et amatkha lifnei bat beliya'al*
Praying drunk is like idol worship
One who wrongly suspected must appease — and bless

children.title: Heart, Lips, Silence — and the Drunk Who May Not Pray
children.gist: Four derivations from a single verse define prayer as inward, articulated with the lips, inaudible to others, and impossible for one who is drunk.

bullets.text: "And Hannah spoke in her heart" — one who prays must direct his heart to his prayer.
"Only her lips moved" — one must enunciate the words with his lips, not merely contemplate them.
"And her voice could not be heard" — it is forbidden to raise one's voice in the *Amidah*.

The balance is unusual: *halakhah* generally wants speech to be audible (as in the discussion of *Shema*), yet prayer is precisely an almost-silent speech — lips moving, no voice. Some *Acharonim* even ask whether thought alone might suffice for *avodah shebalev*; the accepted assumption is that it does not.
"So Eli thought her to be drunk" — from here, that a drunk person is forbidden to pray; that is why Eli rebuked her.
"And Eli said to her: How long will you remain drunk? Remove your wine" — R. Elazar: one who sees an unseemly matter in another must reprimand him.
*Tosafot*: this obligation applies *af al gav deleika issura* — even where the behavior is not technically a violation. Caring about another obliges gentle rebuke.

children.title: "Lo Adoni": Hannah's Reply and Judging Favorably
children.gist: Two versions of Hannah's retort read her "no, my master" as a rebuke of Eli for judging her to guilt rather than to merit.

bullets.text: "And Hannah answered and said: No, my master... I pour out my soul before the Lord" (I Samuel 1:15).
Ulla, and some say R. Yosei son of R. Chanina: she hinted to him — in this matter you are no master, and the Divine Spirit does not rest upon you, since you falsely suspect me.
Another version of her words: are you not a master? Are the *Shekhinah* and the Divine Spirit not with you — that you judged me guilty and did not judge me innocent?
The second version turns the exchange into the obligation to judge another *lekhaf zekhut*: when you see a person acting, tip the scale toward the innocent reading.

A well-known gloss of the Vilna Gaon on how the *kohen gadol* could err: the *urim vetumim* raised the letters *shin, kaf, reish, heh* before Eli, and he read *shikorah*, "drunk," when the message was *kesheirah* — or that she was like Sarah, a barren woman at prayer.

children.title: Clearing Oneself of Suspicion; Drunken Prayer as Idolatry
children.gist: Hannah's denial teaches that the innocent must dispel suspicion, and her phrase *bat beliya'al* yields a verbal analogy equating drunken prayer with idol worship.

bullets.text: "I have drunk neither wine nor liquor" — R. Elazar: one suspected of something of which he is innocent may not rest on his own knowledge; he must inform the suspecter and clear himself.
"Do not take your maidservant as a *bat beliya'al*" (I Samuel 1:16) — R. Elazar: one who prays drunk is as if he engaged in idol worship.
The derivation is a *gezerah shavah*: *beliya'al* here, and *benei beliya'al* in the idolatrous city — "*benei beliya'al* have gone out from your midst" (Devarim 13:14).
Conceptually the link runs deeper: pagan worship often worked through intoxication and induced religious frenzy, so approaching God drunk mimics precisely that distortion of standing before Him.

children.title: Eli Must Appease Her — and Bless Her
children.gist: Eli's "go in peace" and his blessing become the twin obligations of one whose suspicion proved false.

bullets.text: "And Eli answered and said: May you go in peace" (I Samuel 1:17) — R. Elazar: one who suspected another of something he did not do must appease him.
And not only that: he must also bless him — "And may the God of Israel grant your request that you have asked of Him."
Eli does not merely retract; the wrong of a false suspicion is repaired by reconciliation and blessing together.

sections.title: Hannah's Bold Demand: *Tzeva'ot* and the Sotah Threat
sections.gist: Hannah's vow is read as a daring petition — she coins a divine name, presses in like a beggar before a king, and threatens to force God's hand through the *sotah* waters.

children.title: The First to Call God *Tzeva'ot*, and the Parable of the Poor Man
children.gist: Hannah invents the name "Lord of Hosts" to argue that one son is nothing beside all the hosts God created — like a beggar who forces his way to the king's table.

bullets.text: "And she swore an oath and said, Lord of Hosts [*Tzeva'ot*]..." (I Samuel 1:11). R. Elazar: from the day God created His world, no person called Him *Tzeva'ot* until Hannah came and called Him so.
Hannah said before Him: Master of the Universe, of all the hosts and hosts of creations You created in Your world, is it difficult in Your eyes to grant me one son?

Parable: a king made a feast for his servants. A poor man stood at the door and asked for one slice of bread, and they paid him no attention. He pushed in before the king and said: from this whole feast you prepared, is one slice so difficult?
The force of the parable is in the pushing in — the servants would not help, so he went past them straight to the king. That is the posture the Gemara attributes to Hannah's prayer.

children.title: "Im ra'oh tireh": Hannah Threatens the Sotah Waters
children.gist: R. Elazar reads the doubled verb as a threat: if You do not look now, You will be made to see — for I will seclude myself and be vindicated by the *sotah* waters.

bullets.text: On the doubled "*im ra'oh tireh*" — R. Elazar: Hannah said, if You will look upon me now, fine; and if not, in any case You will see.

Her threat: I will go and seclude myself with another man before Elkanah my husband; since I secluded myself they will make me drink the *sotah* water; I will be found innocent, and since You will not make Your Torah false [*pelaster*], I will bear children.
The verse she leans on: "And if the woman was not defiled, but was pure, then she shall be acquitted and she shall conceive" (Bamidbar 5:28).
*Pelaster* derives from the Greek *plastos*, molded or counterfeit: she is saying You will not allow Your own Torah to be exposed as a forgery — and so You will have to give me a child.

children.title: R. Yishmael vs. R. Akiva: What the Sotah Waters Grant
children.gist: The threat only works if the waters make a barren woman conceive — a point disputed in a *baraita*, and per R. Akiva the doubled verb is merely ordinary speech.

bullets.text: The Gemara objects: R. Elazar's reading works for the one who holds that a barren woman is remembered and granted children — but what of the one who holds that the verse promises only easier and better childbearing?
*Baraita*: "then she shall be acquitted and she shall conceive" teaches that if she was barren she will be remembered and granted children — the words of R. Yishmael.
R. Akiva objects: if so, all barren women will go and seclude themselves with other men, and any one who did not in fact sin would be granted children.
R. Akiva therefore reads it as a promise of improved childbirth: pain becomes ease, short children become tall, black become fair, one child becomes two.
According to R. Akiva, what then of Hannah's doubled "*im ra'oh tireh*"? *Dibberah Torah kilshon benei adam* — the Torah speaks in ordinary human idiom, and nothing is derived from the doubling.
R. Akiva's benefits are real but evidently not tempting enough, in his view, to make women manipulate the *sotah* procedure — which is exactly why he rejects R. Yishmael's reading.

sections.title: The Wording of Hannah's Vow
sections.gist: Two phrases in the vow are mined: the threefold "Your maidservant" and the request for "an offspring of men."

children.title: Three Times "Your Maidservant": the Three Mitzvot of Women
children.gist: R. Yosei son of R. Chanina hears in the three *amatekha* Hannah's claim that she never violated the three mitzvot on which a woman's life hangs.

bullets.text: Hannah calls herself "Your maidservant" three times in the vow: "the affliction of Your maidservant... not forget Your maidservant... will give Your maidservant" (I Samuel 1:11).

R. Yosei son of R. Chanina: she said before Him — Master of the Universe, You created three crucibles of death in a woman (some say: three accelerants of death): the *halakhot* of *niddah*, separating *challah*, and lighting the Shabbat lamp.
Her claim: have I ever violated one of them? The word *amatekha* is linked to *mitah*, death.

These three are the mitzvot enumerated as women's in *Bameh Madlikin*, and they map the domestic sphere: the food of the home, the light of the home, and bodily sanctity — with the Mishnah there warning of danger at the hour of childbirth.

children.title: "An Offspring of Men": Four Readings
children.gist: Rav, Shmuel, R. Yochanan and the Rabbis read *zera anashim* as outstanding, as the anointer of two kings, as the equal of two greats, or as utterly ordinary.

bullets.text: "And You will grant Your maidservant an offspring of men" — what is *zera anashim*?
Rav: a man among men — a son who would be outstanding and exceptional.
Shmuel: offspring who will anoint two men to royalty — Saul and David.
R. Yochanan: offspring equivalent to two of the world's greatest — Moses and Aaron, as it is stated "Moses and Aaron among His priests, and Samuel among those who call His name" (Tehillim 99:6).

The Rabbis: offspring inconspicuous among men, who would not stand out at all. When Rav Dimi came he explained: neither too tall nor too short, neither too small nor too fat, neither too white nor too red, neither too smart nor too stupid.
Rashi explains the request for ordinariness as avoiding the evil eye; one may also hear in it Hannah's poignancy — I am not asking for anything special, just a child.

chart.caption: Four readings of *zera anashim*
rows: One who will anoint two men
Equal in worth to two great men
Absorbed among people — average in every way

sections.title: Hannah Returns with Samuel
sections.gist: Her words to Eli a year later yield a law of prayer space, and a startling account of why she had to plead for her son's life.

children.title: "Who Stood Here with You": Four Cubits of Prayer
children.gist: R. Yehoshua ben Levi derives from Eli's standing beside Hannah that one may not sit within four cubits of someone praying.

bullets.text: "My lord, as your soul lives, my lord, I am the woman who stood here with you to pray to the Lord" (I Samuel 1:26).
R. Yehoshua ben Levi: from here, that it is forbidden to sit within four cubits of one who is praying — "who stood here with you" indicates that Eli stood alongside her because she was praying.
*Tosafot*: *imakh* is written full, with a *heh*, implying one may sit from the fifth *amah*; and the prohibition applies at the sides, not only in front.

*Tosafot* cites the *Geonim*: the problem is one who sits idle; one occupied with *Shema*, blessings or the like may sit. Practically, in a crowded synagogue, sitting while engaged in *chazarat hashatz* is not the problematic case — sitting oblivious is.

children.title: Samuel Ruled Before His Teacher — and Hannah Refuses a Replacement
children.gist: R. Elazar reads "for this youth I prayed" as Hannah shielding Samuel from death at the hand of Heaven for ruling on slaughter in Eli's presence.

bullets.text: R. Elazar: Samuel was one who taught *halakhah* in the presence of his teacher; Hannah's "for this youth I prayed" was to protect him from punishment.
The proof text is puzzling: "And they slaughtered the cow and they brought the youth to Eli" (I Samuel 1:25) — what has the one to do with the other?
What happened: Eli told them to call a priest to slaughter the offering. Samuel, seeing them searching, said — why look for a priest? Slaughter by a non-priest is valid.

They brought him before Eli, who asked how he knew. Samuel: is it written "and the priest shall slaughter"? It says "and the priests shall offer" — only from receiving the blood onward is it a priestly mitzvah.
Eli: you have spoken well, but you ruled in your teacher's presence, and anyone who does so — even when the ruling is correct — is liable for death at the hand of Heaven.
The Gemara elsewhere counts this sin among those of Nadav and Avihu, who ruled in the presence of Moses.

Hannah came and shouted before him: "I am the woman who stood here with you" — do not punish the child born of my prayers. Eli: let me punish him, and I will pray that you be granted a son greater than this one. She answered: "For this youth I prayed" — and I want no other.
*Tosafot* asks how Eli was already Samuel's teacher: though the child had not yet studied before him, Eli was the *gadol hador* and Samuel was coming to learn from him, which suffices for the status.
Hannah's refusal of a substitute echoes her earlier request for nothing special: it is this child, irreplaceable — foreshadowing the boy who will hear God's voice while Eli does not.

sections.title: "On Her Heart": Hannah's Argument from Her Own Body
sections.gist: R. Elazar in the name of R. Yosei ben Zimra reads the odd phrase as Hannah arguing that no organ was created in vain — so why these?

bullets.text: "And Hannah spoke *on* her heart" — R. Elazar in the name of R. Yosei ben Zimra: she spoke concerning matters of her heart.

She said before Him: Master of the Universe, of all the organs You created in a woman You created not one in vain — eyes to see, ears to hear, a nose to smell, a mouth to speak, hands to do work, feet to walk, breasts to nurse.
If so, these breasts You placed upon my heart — for what purpose, if not to nurse with them? Grant me a son and I will nurse with them.
The reading takes *al libah*, "on her heart," in its anatomical sense, which is what gives the argument its force: the body You gave me is built for motherhood.

sections.title: Tangent: Fasting on Shabbat
sections.gist: The Gemara appends a second teaching of R. Elazar in the name of R. Yosei ben Zimra — a fast on Shabbat tears up a decree, yet itself requires repair.

bullets.text: R. Elazar in the name of R. Yosei ben Zimra: whoever observes a fast on Shabbat, they tear up and repeal his sentence of seventy years — fasting is harder on Shabbat, when everyone else is feasting.
Nevertheless, he is held accountable for failing to fulfill *oneg Shabbat*.
What is his remedy? Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: he must observe another fast to atone for the fast on Shabbat.

The practical setting is a *ta'anit chalom*, a fast after a disturbing dream, which the *Geonim* hold should be kept at once even on Shabbat; Rashi grounds the efficacy in the sheer difficulty of fasting while others feast.

sections.title: Hannah and Elijah: Words Cast Toward Heaven
sections.gist: R. Elazar reads Hannah's prayer as spoken impertinently *against* God, and pairs her with Elijah, who blamed God for Israel's sin.

bullets.text: R. Elazar: Hannah spoke impertinently toward God on High — *hetichah devarim kelapei ma'alah* — as it says "and she prayed *al* the Lord," rather than the usual "*el* the Lord."

R. Elazar likewise: Elijah spoke impertinently toward Heaven at Mount Carmel — "Answer me, Lord, answer me... and You have turned their hearts backward" (I Kings 18:37), claiming God caused Israel to sin.
R. Shmuel bar R. Yitzchak asks: from where do we know that the Holy One ultimately conceded to Elijah that he was right?

This crystallizes the model of prayer the *sugya* has been building through Hannah: not self-effacing begging but prayer with a *ta'anah*, a claim pressed upon God — the mode later embodied by figures such as R. Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev.

sections.continues: Continues on 32a: the verse showing that God conceded to Elijah, R. Chama son of R. Chanina's three verses without which Israel could not stand, and Moses speaking impertinently toward Heaven.

judgment_calls: The daf opens mid-sentence inside R. Elazar's law of rebuke, so the outline begins with Rav Hamnuna's framing statement at the end of 31a; an alternative was to start at 31b.1 itself, but the derivations are unintelligible without Rav Hamnuna's opening.

The *sotah* dispute of R. Yishmael and R. Akiva could stand as its own top-level section (it is a full tannaitic *machloket* about Bamidbar 5:28); kept under Hannah's bold demand because the Gemara raises it only to test R. Elazar's reading of *im ra'oh tireh*.

The fasting-on-Shabbat teaching is a pure tangent, attached only by the transmission chain R. Elazar in the name of R. Yosei ben Zimra; made a separate top-level section rather than a child of the 'al libah' section, since it shares none of its question.

The four-cubits law and the Samuel story are grouped under 'Hannah returns with Samuel' because both are derived from her two sentences to Eli in I Samuel 1:26–27; they could equally have been split, since one is a law of prayer and the other an aggadah.

The three readings of divine names, the parable and the sotah threat were kept as one top-level bucket ('Hannah's bold demand') because the Gemara presents them as one continuous expansion of her vow.
coverage_notes: Most of the shiur's second half treats material that appears on 32a — R. Chama son of R. Chanina's three verses, Rav Pappa's fourth verse, Moses's *hetiach devarim kelapei ma'alah*, *lekh red*, the parables of the cow and the spoiled son, *vayechal*, releasing God from His vow, the oath to the patriarchs, *salachti kidvarekha*, and Rav Simai on praise before petition. All of that is outside this daf's scope and is not outlined here.
The shiur opens by reviewing the R. Akiva passage on 31a (swaying, communal vs. private prayer); used only as framing in s1, since it belongs to the previous amud.

The essay says the remedy for fasting on Shabbat is to undergo another fast on a subsequent Shabbat; the Sefaria text has Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak requiring a further fast (on a weekday) to atone for the Shabbat fast. Followed the text.

Rav Dimi's list in the essay reads 'not too thin and not too fat, not too fair and not too swarthy'; the text has 'neither too small nor too fat; neither too white nor too red; neither too smart nor too stupid.' Followed the text.
The essay attributes the three-*amatot* teaching to 'R. Yosi bar Chanina'; the text has R. Yosei son of R. Chanina — same sage, text spelling used.
The final unit of the daf (R. Shmuel bar R. Yitzchak's question about God conceding to Elijah) is left open here; the essay supplies the 32a answer, which is recorded only in the 'continues' note.
